title: How a computer works: hardware, software & the boot process
monthTitle: PC Hardware & How Computers Work (A+ Core 1)
summary: See the big picture of a computer: how hardware and software work together, and exactly what happens from the moment you press the power button until the desktop appears.
objectives: Explain the difference between hardware and software in plain terms
Describe the input-process-output-storage model every computer follows
List the main stages of the boot process in order
Identify the role of the BIOS/UEFI firmware and the operating system
Recognise the four core hardware components and what each one does
Use the right vocabulary to describe a computer to a customer or colleague

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the difference between hardware and software?
options: Hardware is the programs; software is the physical parts
Hardware is the physical parts you can touch; software is the instructions that run on it
They are two words for the same thing
Hardware only exists on laptops; software only on desktops
quiz.why: Hardware is the physical equipment (CPU, RAM, drives, screen). Software is the coded instructions, such as the operating system and apps, that tell the hardware what to do.

quiz.q: What is the first piece of code that runs when you press the power button?
options: The firmware (BIOS/UEFI) stored on the motherboard
quiz.why: Before any operating system loads, the motherboard's firmware (BIOS or modern UEFI) runs first. It performs the POST and then locates and hands off to the boot device.

quiz.q: The simple model that describes what every computer does is best summarised as:
quiz.why: Computers take input, process it with the CPU, produce output, and keep data in storage. This four-part model fits everything from a calculator to a server.

quiz.q: What does POST check during boot?
options: That essential hardware like RAM and the CPU is present and working
quiz.why: POST stands for Power-On Self-Test. The firmware quickly checks core hardware before loading the operating system; failures are often signalled by beep codes or on-screen errors.

quiz.q: In your own words, what is the role of the operating system once the computer has booted?
quiz.answer: The operating system manages the hardware and resources and provides a platform so the user and applications can run, giving you a desktop, files, and a way to launch programs.
quiz.why: After firmware hands off, the OS (Windows, macOS, Linux) takes control: it manages memory, the CPU, storage, devices, and presents the interface you actually use.

quiz.q: Name the four core hardware components found in nearly every computer.
quiz.answer: CPU (processor), RAM (memory), storage (drive), and the motherboard, usually powered by a power supply.
quiz.why: These are the essentials: the CPU does the work, RAM holds active data, storage keeps data when powered off, and the motherboard connects everything together.

resources.label: Microsoft Learn — How does a computer work?

body_markdown:
## Hardware vs software

Every computer is two things working together. **Hardware** is the physical equipment you can touch: the processor, memory, drives, screen, keyboard, and the board that links them. **Software** is the set of coded instructions that tells the hardware what to do — the **operating system** and the apps you run.

A useful way to remember it: hardware is the *body*, software is the *thoughts and instructions*. Neither is useful without the other. As a helpdesk technician, half your job is deciding whether a problem is hardware or software, so this distinction matters from day one.

## The model behind every computer

No matter how big or small, a computer follows the same loop: **input → process → output → storage**.

- **Input**: data comes in (keyboard, mouse, microphone, network).
- **Process**: the **CPU** does the calculations and decisions.
- **Output**: results go out (screen, speakers, printer).
- **Storage**: data is kept for later (drive) or held briefly while in use (**RAM**).

A calculator, a phone, and a data-centre server all follow this exact pattern.

## The four core components

Nearly every machine has four essentials:

- **CPU** (the processor) — does the actual work.
- **RAM** (memory) — fast, temporary workspace for whatever is running right now.
- **Storage** (HDD or SSD) — keeps your files when the power is off.
- **Motherboard** — the main board that connects everything, fed by the **power supply**.

We will open each of these up in later lessons. For now, just learn the names.

## The boot process, step by step

When you press the power button, a precise sequence runs:

1. **Power** flows from the power supply to the motherboard.
2. The motherboard **firmware** (**BIOS** on older PCs, **UEFI** on modern ones) starts first.
3. Firmware runs **POST** (Power-On Self-Test) to confirm RAM, CPU and other essentials are present and healthy.
4. Firmware finds the **boot device** (usually the main drive) and loads the **bootloader**.
5. The bootloader starts the **operating system**.
6. The OS loads drivers and shows you the **login screen** and **desktop**.

If POST fails, you may hear **beep codes** or see an error before any OS appears — a strong clue the problem is hardware.

## BIOS/UEFI and the operating system

Think of **firmware** as the building's caretaker who unlocks the doors and checks the lights work, then hands the keys to the **operating system** — the manager who actually runs the place. You can usually enter firmware settings by tapping a key like **Del**, **F2**, or **F10** right after powering on.

You can confirm key system facts from inside Windows once it boots:

```powershell
systeminfo | findstr /B /C:"OS Name" /C:"System Type" /C:"BIOS Version"
```

## Your task

Watch a computer boot and narrate the stages out loud. Power on a PC and tap the firmware key (often **Del** or **F2**) to peek at the BIOS/UEFI screen, then exit without changing anything. Once Windows loads, open PowerShell, run the `systeminfo` command above, and write down the OS name, system type, and BIOS version. In two sentences, describe what happened between pressing power and seeing the desktop.

slides.title: How a computer works: hardware, software & the boot process
slides.sub: Month 1 - PC Hardware & How Computers Work (A+ Core 1)  |  Lesson 1
slides.narration: Welcome to the very first lesson of your journey from no experience to a Tier Two helpdesk technician. Today we build the foundation everything else rests on: what a computer actually is, how hardware and software work together, and exactly what happens from the moment you press the power button until the desktop appears. Take it slowly. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to describe a computer with confidence.

slides.title: Hardware vs software
bullets: Hardware: the physical parts you can touch.
Software: the coded instructions that run on it.
Hardware is the body, software is the thoughts.
Your job often starts with: hardware or software?
slides.narration: Let's start with the biggest idea in computing. A computer is two things working together. Hardware is the physical equipment you can touch, like the processor, the memory, and the screen. Software is the set of instructions that tells that hardware what to do, like the operating system and your apps. A nice way to remember it: hardware is the body, software is the thoughts. As a helpdesk tech, one of your first questions is always, is this a hardware problem or a software problem?

slides.title: The model every computer follows
bullets: Input: data comes in.
Process: the C P U does the work.
Output: results go out.
Storage: data is kept for later.
slides.narration: No matter how big or small, every computer follows the same simple loop. Input, where data comes in from the keyboard or mouse. Process, where the C P U does the calculations. Output, where the results go out to the screen or speakers. And storage, where data is kept. A calculator, a phone, and a giant server all follow this exact same pattern. Learn this loop and you understand the heart of computing.

slides.title: The four core components
bullets: CPU: the processor that does the work.
RAM: fast temporary workspace.
Storage: keeps files when power is off.
Motherboard: connects everything together.
slides.narration: Nearly every machine has four essential parts. The C P U, or processor, does the actual work. The RAM, or memory, is a fast temporary workspace for whatever is running right now. Storage, like a hard drive or solid state drive, keeps your files even when the power is off. And the motherboard is the main board that connects everything together, fed by the power supply. We'll open each of these up in the lessons ahead. For now, just learn the names.

slides.title: Press power: what happens first
bullets: Power flows from the supply to the motherboard.
Firmware (BIOS or UEFI) runs first, before any OS.
It lives on a chip on the motherboard.
BIOS is older; UEFI is modern.
slides.narration: So you press the power button. What runs first? Not Windows, not your apps. The first code to run is the firmware that lives on a chip on the motherboard. On older machines this is called the BIOS, and on modern machines it's called U E F I. Think of firmware as the caretaker who unlocks the building before the manager arrives. It runs before any operating system exists.

slides.title: POST: the self-check
bullets: POST means Power-On Self-Test.
Firmware checks RAM, CPU and essentials.
Failures give beep codes or error messages.
A failed POST usually means hardware trouble.
slides.narration: The next thing the firmware does is run something called POST, which stands for Power-On Self-Test. This is a quick health check that confirms the essential hardware, like the RAM and the C P U, is present and working. If something is wrong, you'll often hear a pattern of beeps, called beep codes, or see an error message on screen. Here's a useful clue: if a PC fails during POST, before you ever see Windows, the problem is almost always hardware.

slides.title: Finding the boot device
bullets: Firmware locates the boot device, usually the main drive.
It loads a small program called the bootloader.
The bootloader starts the operating system.
You can change boot order in firmware settings.
slides.narration: Once POST passes, the firmware looks for the boot device, which is usually your main drive. On that drive it finds a small program called the bootloader, whose only job is to start the operating system. If you've ever booted a PC from a USB stick, that's you telling the firmware to use a different boot device. You can change this order inside the firmware settings, which you reach by tapping a key like Del or F two right after powering on.

slides.title: The operating system takes over
bullets: Firmware hands the keys to the OS.
The OS loads drivers for your hardware.
It manages memory, CPU, storage and devices.
Then it shows the login screen and desktop.
slides.narration: Now the operating system, like Windows, takes over. If firmware was the caretaker, the operating system is the manager who actually runs the place. It loads drivers so it can talk to your hardware, it manages the memory and the C P U and the storage, and finally it presents the login screen and the desktop you actually use. From this point on, almost everything you touch is software running on top of the OS.

slides.title: Check it for yourself
bullets: Tap Del or F2 at startup to view firmware.
In Windows, PowerShell shows system facts.
Note the OS name, system type and BIOS version.
Knowing your tools builds confidence.
slides.narration: Let's make this real. When your PC starts, tap a key like Del or F two to peek at the firmware screen, then exit without changing anything. Once Windows loads, open PowerShell and run the command on screen. It uses systeminfo piped into findstr to pull out just the OS name, the system type, and the BIOS version. Don't worry about the exact syntax yet; just see that the tools to inspect your machine are right there waiting for you.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Hardware is physical; software is instructions.
Computers follow input, process, output, storage.
Boot order: power, firmware, POST, bootloader, OS.
Task: watch a boot and run systeminfo.
slides.narration: Let's recap. A computer is hardware, the physical parts, and software, the instructions. Every computer follows the loop of input, process, output, and storage. And when you press power, the order is: power flows in, firmware runs, POST checks the hardware, the bootloader loads, and then the operating system takes over. Your task before the next lesson: watch a computer boot and narrate the stages out loud, peek at the firmware screen, then run the systeminfo command in PowerShell and write down what you find. Great start. I'll see you in lesson two, where we open the case.
